name: Salla disease
aliases: Free sialic acid storage disease, Finnish type

clinicalPearls: Salla disease is an autosomal recessive free sialic acid storage disorder caused by variants in SLC17A5, which encodes sialin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports free sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) from the lysosome to the cytosol.
It represents the milder, later-onset and slowly progressive end of the free sialic acid storage disease spectrum; the severe infantile form (ISSD) lies at the other end and is allelic.
It is markedly enriched in the Finnish population owing to a founder missense variant, hence its origin in the Salla region, although cases occur worldwide.
Typical presentation is in infancy with hypotonia, nystagmus and delayed motor milestones, evolving into ataxia, spasticity, intellectual disability and dysarthria over childhood.
Brain MRI characteristically shows hypomyelination and a thin, hypoplastic corpus callosum, reflecting the central hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy.

The biochemical hallmark is greatly increased free (unconjugated) sialic acid in urine and in cultured fibroblasts, distinguishing it from sialidosis, where bound/oligosaccharide-linked sialic acid accumulates.
Unlike infantile sialic acid storage disease, coarse features, visceromegaly, dysostosis and fetal hydrops are usually absent or mild in classic Salla disease.
Diagnosis combines raised urinary free sialic acid with SLC17A5 molecular testing; enzyme assays are not diagnostic because the defect is in transport, not degradation.
reference.pathophysiology: SLC17A5 (chromosome 6q13) encodes sialin, a proton-driven transporter in the lysosomal membrane that carries free sialic acid, generated by lysosomal breakdown of sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids, out of the lysosome into the cytosol for reuse or excretion. In Salla disease hypomorphic variants, classically the Finnish founder missense allele, retain partial transporter activity, so free sialic acid accumulates progressively within enlarged lysosomes across many tissues, especially the central nervous system. The consequences are twofold: intralysosomal storage distends cells and disrupts function, and impaired cytosolic delivery of sialic acid limits its availability for re-sialylation of glycoconjugates important for myelin membranes. The result is a central hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy with a thin corpus callosum and cerebral and cerebellar involvement, producing the progressive motor, cognitive and cerebellar signs. The severity of disease tracks with residual sialin function: near-complete loss produces the severe infantile phenotype with prenatal onset, hydrops, organomegaly and early death, whereas partial function produces the attenuated, slowly progressive Salla phenotype. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Infantile free sialic acid storage disease (severe allelic SLC17A5 phenotype)
Sialidosis (neuraminidase deficiency) and galactosialidosis, in which bound sialic acid accumulates
Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease and other hypomyelinating leukodystrophies (e.g. PMLD, 4H/POLR3-related)
Other lysosomal storage disorders presenting with hypotonia and regression
Cerebral palsy or non-progressive hypotonia in early presentations
additionalInvestigations: Urinary free (unconjugated) sialic acid quantification, markedly elevated
Free sialic acid measurement in cultured skin fibroblasts
SLC17A5 molecular genetic testing, including the Finnish founder variant where relevant
Brain MRI for hypomyelination and thin corpus callosum
Nerve conduction and evoked potential studies where clinically indicated
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment for baseline and monitoring
Exclusion of sialidosis/galactosialidosis via oligosaccharide and enzyme studies
redFlags: Progressive loss of previously acquired motor or cognitive skills
Worsening spasticity or bulbar dysfunction affecting swallowing and airway safety
New seizures or acute neurological deterioration
Feeding difficulty with failure to thrive
Rapid early decline suggesting the severe infantile phenotype rather than classic Salla disease
reference.prognosis: Classic Salla disease is slowly progressive and compatible with survival into adulthood, though with significant intellectual disability and motor disability; the allelic severe infantile form carries a poor prognosis with early death. Management is supportive, as no disease-modifying therapy is currently available.
pitfalls: Confusing Salla disease with sialidosis; the two differ fundamentally in whether free or bound sialic acid accumulates
Ordering enzyme assays expecting a degradative defect, when the underlying problem is lysosomal transport
Mistaking the hypomyelination and thin corpus callosum for another hypomyelinating leukodystrophy without measuring urinary free sialic acid
Labelling early hypotonia as non-progressive cerebral palsy and missing the metabolic diagnosis
Assuming absence of Finnish ancestry excludes the diagnosis, when cases occur in many populations
references: Standard metabolic medicine and lysosomal storage disorder references
Clinical and paediatric neurology reference texts
management: Supportive, symptom-directed care as no disease-modifying therapy exists for this free sialic acid storage disorder
Antispasticity agents such as baclofen for the evolving spasticity, with physiotherapy to maintain mobility and posture
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures where these develop
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia, ataxia and motor disability, with mobility aids and orthoses
Nutritional and feeding support, including safe swallowing assessment as bulbar function declines
Developmental support, special education and speech and language therapy for the intellectual disability and dysarthria
Multidisciplinary neurology and metabolic follow-up with baseline and serial developmental assessment
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SLC17A5 disorder, with carrier testing of relatives
